title: Apple's iCloud Private Relay Can Actually Expose Your Real IP Address
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 6, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: picture alliance via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            As 404 Media reports, flaws in Apple’s web browser engine allow IP addresses to be revealed when they're supposed to be hidden.
                                            Web requests are made outside of the browser and the protections of Private Relay, meaning that websites that support passkeys can see users' real IP addresses
                                            If you want to keep your IP address hidden and your data encrypted across all apps and browsers on your device, you may want to consider a separate VPN.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you use iCloud Private Relay, Apple's paid IP address masking service, your internet browsing activity may not actually be private. As 404 Media reports, flaws in Apple’s web browser engine allow IP addresses to be revealed, either maliciously or incidentally, even when they're supposed to be hidden. How Private Relay is exposing IP addressesiCloud Private Relay, which is part of Apple's iCloud+ subscription, is supposed to keep both who you are and what sites you visit hidden when you are browsing in Safari. Without it, your network provider and the websites you view can see your IP address and DNS records, which can be used to track your location and browsing history over time. Private Relay is supposed to encrypt DNS records and generate a temporary IP address, keeping any single party, including Apple, from obtaining both. The issue, discovered by security researchers Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk, is related to how passkeys work. Web requests are made outside of the browser and the protections of Private Relay, meaning that websites that support passkeys can see users' real IP addresses. Obviously, this impacts Safari traffic, but researchers found the issue in Onion Browser, an iOS app that encrypts traffic through the Tor network. Both 404 Media and TechCrunch verified the issue in their own tests. 
The researchers stated that they informed Apple but haven't been given a timeline for when the vulnerability will be addressed. Apple is generally pretty good on privacy issues, but this isn't the first to arise in recent months. In July, "Hide My Email," the company's email masking service, was revealed to have a vulnerability that actually exposed users' real email addresses. Apple reportedly knew about it for over a year and claimed to have patched it—but it hadn't. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
While Private Relay can be a useful privacy tool—if it works as intended—it's not a true VPN (Virtual Private Network) because it only provides protection when browsing in Safari. If you want to keep your IP address hidden and your data encrypted across all apps and browsers on your device, you may want to consider a separate VPN service.

            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor

            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        The global memory crisis—commonly referred to as RAMageddon—continues to make just about every piece of tech more expensive. Even Apple, a $4.5 trillion company, can't weather the markets without raising prices. What's more, Apple is struggling to produce enough Macs to meet demand, as you might discover if you try to buy a MacBook Air right now. While it's always a good idea to consider buying used tech, it now makes more sense than ever.As it happens, if you're in the market for Apple's "budget" Mac, the MacBook Neo, it's an excellent time to buy used. Apple originally released the MacBook Neo for $599, a fantastic price for a complete Mac experience. But since the RAM shortage, the company increased its starting price to $699—not bad, but certainly not as enticing an offer as it was at its release just five months ago. The MacBook Neo hits the Apple Refurbished Store But now, the MacBook Neo is officially available directly from Apple at its original $599 price point—as long as you buy it refurbished. But unlike buying a used piece of tech from a friend or a random outlet, Apple's refurbished store isn't unlike buying products new: The company says that it puts "Certified Refurbished" products through a "rigorous" refurbishment process, which includes testing, cleaning, and repackaging. Refurbished Apple products also have the same one-year limited warranty of new products, as well as a 14-day return policy, and you can purchase AppleCare if you so choose. As such, buying a MacBook Neo on the refurbished store should be just about the same experience as buying one new—except for the fact you have an additional $100 in your wallet. You get the same A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM, 13-inch display, 256GB SSD, and two USB ports (one USB 3 and one USB 2). If you want additional storage, as well as an embedded Touch ID sensor, you can upgrade to the 512GB model, also refurbished for $679.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
As tech gets more expensive, and companies make fewer products to sell, it makes sense to check out Apple's Refurbished Store for other devices, too. Just about every product category is represented here, to take a look before you buy a device at its full (and inflated) price.

title: How to Protect Yourself From This Massive Ongoing Cryptocurrency Hack
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zooey Liao/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Bad actors have managed to steal more than $130 million in cryptocurrency from offline hardware wallets.
                                            Coldcard wallets had a vulnerability allowing hackers to brute-force users' seed phrases.
                                            Users should update their firmware and migrate to a new seed phrase.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It seems no sooner does someone come up with a method to keep your digital data safe than hackers find a way to subvert it. Today's case in point: Bad actors have stolen more than $130 million in cryptocurrency from users of offline hardware wallets, devices specifically meant to be a safe option for securing bitcoin. Hackers are attacking cold crypto walletsAs TechCrunch reports, multiple groups of hackers have gained access to Coldcard crypto wallets and are continuing to drain funds in an ongoing theft. The wallets, made by Coinkite, are considered "cold," meaning they are not connected to the internet or any other device, and users' keys or seed phrases exist entirely offline. By contrast, "hot" wallets are connected to the internet and include apps and browser extensions. Typically, hot wallets are considered a greater security risk for hacks, theft, malware, and ransomware, but this latest attack exploited a flaw in Coldcard's seed phrase generation process, compromising users' cold wallets. The vulnerability made seeds predictable, so threat actors were able to brute-force victims' passwords—essentially, guess them via trial and error—and gain access to their wallets. 
Hackers carried out more than 200 crypto attacks between January and July of this year, leading to losses of $972 million. That's an increase in the number of events, but a significantly lower amount stolen, compared to the first six months of 2025. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to protect your cryptocurrency wallet According to Coinkite's security advisory, the vulnerability has now been patched for all affected firmware, so users should first install available updates to their devices from the official download pages (linked in the advisory). Users should also migrate their wallets to a new seed phrase following the specific instructions in the advisory. While using a cold wallet should provide greater protection, you may also consider a diversified storage strategy for your cryptocurrency and leave minimal assets in hot wallets at any given time. That way, if one is compromised, it doesn't leave everything vulnerable.

title: Here's When Google Assistant Is Leaving Android
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 5, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Didem Mente/Anadolu via Getty Images)
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google Assistant is officially leaving Android. The company has started contacting existing users with the news.
                                            Google says that it will start removing Google Assistant from Android devices starting Sept. 4, though it will take a few weeks in total.
                                            This deprecation affects Android devices and Wear OS smartwatches, as well as some Android Auto cars.
                                            Google built-in cars, Google TV devices, and Google Home speakers and smart displays can continue using Google Assistant past Sept. 4.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        For the longest time, Google Assistant was the bot to beat. While those of us in the Apple ecosystem have struggled to get Siri to follow our commands, Google Assistant could answer almost any query you had. It led the charge on conversational AI, which let you ask a follow-up without needing to restate the original question in full. I've never been one to rely much on assistants, but I'll admit that I've wished Siri could be a bit more like Google Assistant over the years.Of course, Google Assistant isn't Google's assistant of choice these days. Since March of 2024, the company has let users swap out Google Assistant for Gemini, Google's flagship AI platform. Then, just one year later, the company officially replaced its popular bot with Gemini across its platforms and services. Google didn't outright kill off Google Assistant then and there; you've been able to use it if you wish, but it did say it would require Google Assistant at some point in 2025. 2025 has come and gone, and Google Assistant is still here, but that won't be the case for long.    Google Assistant has an official end-of-life dateAs reported by 9to5Google, Google Assistant will officially begin shutting down on Friday, Sept. 4. The company alerted some Google Assistant users via email, letting them know that Google Assistant is being discontinued, and Gemini, "our next-generation AI-powered assistant," is now the official Android assistant. On that date, Google says it will begin removing access to Google Assistant from devices, though it may take "a few weeks to reach everyone." That means you may still have access to Google Assistant through the third week in September, though you could lose access at any point. 
This Google Assistant end-of-life doesn't just apply to Android smartphones and tablets. Google says it will also revoke its legacy assistant from Wear OS watches, headphones, and Android Auto—at least when the feature is powered by the user's smartphone. Google says that "Google built-in" cars will still be able to use Google Assistant after Sept. 4.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Which devices will Google Assistant still work with?At this time, Google TV devices and Google Home speakers and smart displays still have access to Google Assistant. However, in some cases, it seems you cannot revert back to Google Assistant if you choose to use Gemini on your device.

title: Apple Just Blocked Hackers From Taking Advantage of This Serious Security Flaw
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 6, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just released three security updates for macOS that all patch the same serious security vulnerability.
                                            macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, and macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 all patch a flaw that can allow hackers to enable Screen Sharing without permission.
                                            It's possible this flaw could let hackers not only see your Mac's screen, but also take over your computer entirely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple released three new security updates for Macs on Thursday, Aug. 6. You don't need to be running the latest version, macOS 26, to take advantage of these updates, either. While the company does have a new Tahoe update, Apple's security updates here include releases for both macOS 15 Sequoia and macOS 14 Sonoma as well—and all of these updates are aimed at patching a flaw that would let hackers share your screen without your permission.Apple's latest macOS security patches fix a  Screen Sharing vulnerability macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, and macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 all contain the same, singular security patch: Tracked as CVE-2026-65400, this fix is for a Screen Sharing flaw that Apple says could allow an attacker on your network to "authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials." In layman's terms, this security flaw could let hackers activate Screen Sharing without permission, which would leave the contents of your Mac's display totally open to anyone in the know.Apple's Screen Sharing feature is complex, which is good for usability but potentially dangerous in this case. Not only can people using Screen Sharing see your Mac's display, they can, if prompted, take over your Mac as well. Typically, this requires permissions on both sides to activate, and it's not clear whether that functionality is impacted by this security flaw. But if it is, a bad actor could also theoretically take control of your computer using this flaw—accessing your files, messages, or anything else on your Mac.
The good news is Apple did not say that this flaw was previously publicly disclosed or being actively exploited. As such, chances are good that no hackers out there are currently taking advantage of it. However, that doesn't mean it's an impossibility: Certain AI models, like Claude Mythos, are adept at discovering security vulnerabilities, so hypothetically, someone out there could have found this flaw before Apple did. Luckily, the patch is now out for anyone running the latest three versions of macOS, so all you have to do to protect yourself is update your Mac.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to install this Screen Sharing security patch on Mac  Whether your Mac is brand new or a few versions behind, there's a very good chance you can install one of these security patches. To do so, open System Settings > General > Software Update, let macOS look for the update, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install it.

body:
Joel Cunningham
                            
        
            Joel Cunningham
                
                                            Deputy Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJoel Cunningham is Lifehacker’s Deputy Editor. He has 15 years of experience as a writer and editor. Previously, he was managing editor of content marketing for Barnes & Noble, where he founded the Barnes & Noble Sci-Fi & Fantasy Blog.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
            Deal pricing and availability subject to change after time of publication.
    
            Credit: Lifehacker / Xteink
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        The tech world is usually all about selling you the bigger, better, newer model every year, so I still find it funny that the most talked-about e-reader of 2026 isn't a flashy new Kindle or a pricey Boox tablet, but a tiny, cheap e-ink device from an upstart Chinese tech company. Xteink makes e-readers small enough to fit in your pocket—any pocket—an irresistible form factor that has garnered them a devoted online following despite their slightly janky software.The Xteink X4 was my own personal tech upgrade of the year for 2025, and this year's smaller X3 and more fully-featured X4 Pro are even better. Every time I'm using one of them in public, I get asked what it is and where I got it, and I can't stop recommending them to people looking to find more ways to reduce their doomscrolling and read more books. If that's you, it's the time to buy, because today only Xteink is offering 15% off on both the X4 and the X3—and the latter was already marked down 13%, so the additional discount takes it to its lowest price ever.
Given the discount takes both devices down to the same sub-$60 price, if you're not sure which one to buy, there's really only one factor to consider: The Xteink X4 is pretty small—with a 4.3-inch screen, it's roughly the size of a small wallet—while the 3.7-inch X3 is even smaller, roughly the size of a credit card. Otherwise, the devices are fairly similar, the biggest differences being slightly better resolution on the X3 (thanks solely to the smaller screen increasing the number of pixels per inch) and different charging cables (in order to maximize space, the X3 charges with an included pogo pin adapter, while the X4 uses USB-C). 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Personally, I like the X3 better, as the smaller screen is still comfortable to read on, and it's so small I often forget I'm carrying it—until I need to pull it out to read while I wait for the subway, so I can avoid looking at my phone.

title: Google Docs Is Rolling Out These Three New Gemini Features
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 30, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google is rolling out new Gemini features in Google Docs for select users.
                                            Gemini can now generate and edit images directly in Google Docs, pulling from the context of your doc.
                                            Gemini can also generate and edit multiple images at once, based on the prompt.
                                            The features are rolling out now to Workspace users, including Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subcribers.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Google makes both Gemini and Docs, so it's not surprising that you'll find plenty of the former's features while using the latter. Gemini has a ton of Google Docs integration, including reading your text out loud, searching and summarizing your Docs in Drive, and a "Gemini bar" embedded into the app for prompting anytime. It's to the point that it's tough to avoid, which isn't great news for Google Docs users uninterested in AI features. Of course, that won't stop Google. The company continues to add new Gemini features at a steady clip, and this week is no exception. As Android Authority notes, Gemini is now rolling out new image creation and editing abilities available directly in Google Docs. Google announced the changes in a Workspace update on Tuesday, highlighting how Docs users can tap into Gemini to create and edit images, diagrams, and infographics in their documents. According to Google, Gemini has three new functions Workspace users can take advantage of. First, users can create infographics or diagrams that summarize the doc in question. You could ask Gemini to do something like "add a diagram that explains the proposal at the top of this doc," or "create an infographic that summarizes the doc visually." Google says Gemini will pull from the context of the doc for these graphics, so these images should reflect what you have written in your doc—excluding the odd hallucination, of course.
In addition, Gemini can "refine existing visuals." You can ask Gemini to adjust the images in your doc with requests like, "change the aspect ratio of this image to 4:3," or "match the image's style to the other images in this doc." Finally, you can also ask Gemini to generate or edit multiple images at once. You could request the AI to create infographics in each section of your doc, or update all images at once.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Who has access to these new Gemini features?These new additions to Google Docs aren't rolling out to everyone. Instead, they're exclusive to Workspace users, which includes Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. If you pay for Google's AI features, you can try these out once they roll out on your end. If your school, work, or organization uses Workspace, the same applies. Here's the full list:Business: Business Standard and PlusEnterprise: Enterprise Standard, and PlusEducation: Education PlusConsumer: Google AI Pro and UltraEducation Add-ons: Google AI Pro for Education; Teaching and Learning

title: WhatsApp Just Added Five New Group Chat Features, Including '@All'
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        August 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Image
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            WhatsApp is rolling out five new features and changes for group chats.
                                            There's now an "@all" function that lets you alert the whole group at once, even if users have the group muted.
                                            There are three new changes to how polls work in group chats on WhatsApp, including the ability to edit polls after posting.
                                            You can also create new group chats from existing groups, for times you need to sidebar with select members of the chat.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        On Tuesday, WhatsApp announced a handful of new features and changes for its app. But unlike the usual feature updates, these changes are specifically for group chats. In total, WhatsApp has five new updates for your groups, one of which will make it much easier to get the entire chat's attention. Here's what's new:  WhatsApp finally gets an "@all" function
    
            
            
                                        Credit: WhatsApp
                    
    
If you've ever used Slack, Google Chat, or any messaging platform with an "@all" function, you know how useful (and potentially disruptive) it can be. By typing "@all" as part of your message, you can force everyone in the group chat to receive a notification for your text. It's especially useful for time-sensitive messages, since it lets you skip tagging all group members one by one. Of course, "@all" can be overused and abused. No one wants unnecessary alerts, but this feature increases the risk that you'll be bothered by someone who didn't think through their "@all" use all that carefully—particularly since the feature breaks through muted group chats. Luckily, there is a notification setting that will let you choose to mute even @all alerts—though keep in mind you'll miss out on these all of those alerts going forward. While @all is available to all group chat members, WhatsApp notes the feature is limited to admins in groups of more than 32 people.   
WhatsApp's group polls now have three new featuresPolls are something I don't use enough in my chat apps. They're a great way to gauge your groups' opinions on any number of topics, from where to go for dinner to which movie you should all see. Now, WhatsApp says it is making polls "even more useful" by adding three new changes to the mix:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You can now set an end time for polls to close, so users have a deadline to respond by. If the poll is particularly sensitive, you can hide responders' names, so people can vote more freely.Finally, you can edit poll questions within 15 minutes of posting, in case you made a mistake or need to make a question clearer.  You can create new WhatsApp group chats from existing groups
    
            
            
                                        Credit: WhatsApp
                    
    
The next time you need to create a smaller group chat featuring members of an existing group, you no longer need to build it from scratch. Instead, you can make new group chats from your current groups, which should make splitting off much easier. WhatsApp sees this as a great way to "plan a surprise party" or "coordinate event logistics," but we all know this is going to be used in, let's say, less kind ways. Yes, the ability to create a side chat from a main chat will be used to talk smack inconspicuously. (I imagine the first text in these breakout group chats will be "Oh my god, can you believe they just said that?")

title: How to Stop Scammers From Showing You Ads on Your Android After Every Phone Call
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 29, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're an Android user who is seeing ads pop up after your phone calls, you need not assume this is some new feature you have to learn to live with. It's actually an ad fraud scam, and you can do something about it. Researchers have identified dozens of apps on the Google Play Store that are able to display ads on top of the Android phone interface, a scheme known as AfterCall. How ads are taking over Android callsThis scam originates with seemingly harmless utility apps downloaded from the Google Play Store, such as calendars, alarm clocks, and notepads. When installed, they request overlay permissions, which allow them to appear on top of other apps—and thus display ads over phone calls. These apps can detect when a call ends and will then launch full-screen ads wrapped in a fake call info screen. Since it looks like they are simply part of the call interface, users may be less likely to suspect that they are actually malicious. It's worth noting that overlay permissions can't be granted via a standard pop-up during the app installation process. They are a type of "special permission" that requires users to go into their system settings to enable. Android apps are supposed to request these permissions in context and give a clear reason for doing so. AfterCall scammers are using justifications like alarms not being able to go off or appear correctly without overlay permissions, though some apps will simply crash if users decline permissions.
How to remove AfterCall adsBecause the ads appear out of context—after a phone call and with content unrelated to the utility app—it's harder for users to figure out what's causing them. The utility apps aren't obviously malicious and don't appear on recent app lists when ads are displayed, so it's not obvious that they are connected to the problem. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you are seeing ads pop up after phone calls on your Android, check for apps that have overlay permissions. Go to Settings > Apps > Special app access (this may be hidden behind a three-dot menu) and click on the permission type. Look for apps you don't recognize, or which shouldn't have "display on top" permissions, and uninstall them. You should regularly audit these permissions, and disable any that aren't essential. On the user side, these apps seem to be mostly an annoyance rather than outright malicious programs that are harvesting your sensitive data, though installing any program that requests unnecessary permissions can introduce significant risk. If nothing else, however, these apps do appear to waste brands' advertising dollars and could damage their reputation with users—but you probably just care about how to stop seeing them after your calls.

title: Your Samsung Galaxy Watch's Browser Just Got a Useful Upgrade
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 31, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Bloomberg / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            If you have a Galaxy Watch, the latest version of Samsung Browser is a bit more like a desktop web browser than before.
                                            Once you update your browser, you'll be able to download images from webpages directly to your watch.
                                            There are limited supported file types, and the image needs to be 10MB or smaller.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Full disclosure: I'm all-in on the Apple ecosystem, and I don't necessarily plan to switch anytime soon—but that doesn't mean I don't peek at what could be. I have few complaints about my aging Apple Watch, but, I'll admit, Android smartwatches can be pretty cool. While I don't think I'd be doing a whole lot of web browsing on my watch, the fact that the Galaxy Watch has a dedicated browser is a great feature. (For the uninitiated: Apple Watches have a built-in web browser that only appears when watchOS deems a search relevant. There is no Safari app for the Apple Watch.)If you have a Galaxy Watch, you probably already know you can install Samsung Browser on your device. What you might not know, however, is that your wearable web browser just got an excellent upgrade that makes it function even more like a desktop web browser. As reported by SamMobile, Samsung Browser for Galaxy Watch now lets you download images from webpages. That means if you stumble across a picture on the web, you can download it directly to your Galaxy Watch, rather than switch to your phone, tablet, or computer to save it.How to download images on your Galaxy Watch's Samsung BrowserFirst, update Samsung Browser to its latest version, then open it and navigate to a webpage of your choosing. When you find an image you want to download, long-press on the image, and you'll see a new "Download Image" option. Tap it, and your image will save on your watch. You can find all downloaded images in the "Downloads" folder on the Samsung Browser home page. 
SamMobile notes that this option doesn't seem to work until the website has fully loaded. As such, you may need to wait a bit longer than you might expect before you're able to download an image. In addition, there are some limitations: You can download PNG, JPEG, JPG, and GIFs up to 10MB. If you come across a different file type, or the image in question is too large, you won't be able to download it. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
This should work on any Galaxy Watch that can run the latest version of Samsung Browser. However, if you're in the market for an upgrade, Samsung recently announced the Galaxy Watch 9 at its July Unpacked event. The watch is due out Aug. 7, so you can preorder it now or wait until it comes out to see if older Galaxy Watches come down in price.

body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 7, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Made by Google/YouTube
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Made by Google 2026, Google's annual hardware keynote, is nearly here.
                                            Google confirmed that we'll see next-generation Pixel smartphones, like the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
                                            We may also see the new Pixel Watch 5 and perhaps the Google Pixel Tag.
                                            Made by Google 2026 kicks off 3 p.m. PT on Wednesday, Aug. 6.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        It's nearly time for another Google keynote. Back in May, the company hosted Google I/O, its annual developers conference, where it announced a series of new software features and AI updates. On the flip side, "Made by Google" is all about the hardware that will run those new software updates. If you're curious about Google's next generation of devices, you'll want to tune into this presentation. When is Made by Google 2026?Usually, tech events—especially in the U.S.—are in the morning for West Coasters (and, as such, in the early afternoon for East Coasters). Many companies like Google are based in California, so a 10 a.m. PT start time is pretty common. As I'm on the East Coast, I'm quite used to starting coverage around 1 p.m. for most tech events. This year is much different. Made by Google officially kicks off at 3 p.m. PT on Wednesday, Aug. 12. That means a 6 p.m. start time for those of us on the East Coast.  
Where can you watch Made by Google 2026?If you didn't get an invite to watch Made by Google in person, no worries: The company hosts a livestream for anyone to watch from home. Most companies run a livestream through YouTube, and as Google owns the video platform, it makes sense for its official livestream to live there, too. Even though the event doesn't start until next week, Google already has the livestream video open. You can watch from the feed below, or from the link here. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What will Google announce at Made by Google 2026?While most companies officially keep their product announcements under wraps prior to an event, these days leaks and rumors typically spill the beans long before it kicks off. Perhaps that's why Google has gone ahead and spoiled the biggest announcements ahead of time: The company has already posted teasers for both the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro Fold on social media. While even those reveals were hardly a surprise to anyone following the Google rumors, it is funny to have confirmation about two products ahead of time. In addition to new Pixel smartphones, rumors suggest that we'll also see the new Pixel Watch 5 on Wednesday. Perhaps the company will even announce the Google Pixel Tag, which would mark Google's first attempt at an AirTag-like product. For a full account of the leaks and rumors going into Made by Google 2026, check out our explainer here.

title: 10 Hacks Every Google Drive User Should Know
description: As the hub for (almost) all files stored in your Google Account, Drive is a critical tool for Workspace users to save, organize, and
body:
As the hub for (almost) all files stored in your Google Account, Drive is a critical tool for Workspace users to save, organize, and share documents, spreadsheets, and media. To keep your Drive organized and make the most of its collaboration features, use these 10 hidden hacks.  Add shortcuts instead of duplicating files to save storage spaceIf you're organizing Drive and need a single file to be accessible from multiple folders—such as across several projects—you don't need to move it or create multiple copies, which takes up storage space and prevents collaborators across separate teams from working in the same live version. Instead, leave the original where it is and create shortcuts in other locations. Right-click on any Drive file to bring up the options menu, then go to Organize > Add shortcut and select the destination folder. Use URL shortcuts to quickly create account-specific new filesURL shortcuts are huge timesavers for launching new Drive files—Docs, Sheets, and Slides specifically—especially if you're logged into multiple Google Accounts, such as work and personal, at the same time. When you type doc.new, sheet.net, or slide.new into your address bar, a new file will automatically be created under your primary account. Add /1, /2, /3 etc. to specify which account you want to use. This prevents multiple clicks just to get a new file started. 
Another URL shortcut allows you to force shared file recipients to create a copy rather than gaining view or edit access to the original. This is handy for sharing templates, checklists, and other materials that users will need to edit while preserving the master version. Simply replace /edit or /view at the end of the sharing link with /copy, and recipients will be prompted to "Make a Copy" upon opening. Upload new versions to overwrite existing docs without changing the sharing linkNative Google files update in real time when edited, allowing all collaborators to see changes, but new versions of PDFs, images, and videos have to be reshared—unless you overwrite the original. Right-click on any non-Google file and go to Manage versions > Upload new version to keep the same sharing link for the update. Lock files in read-only mode to prevent further editsIf you want to share the final version of a Drive file but prevent recipients from making edits—either accidentally or on purpose—you can lock it in read-only mode. This is quicker than turning it into a PDF or managing permissions for different users. Right-click on the file to pull up the options menu, then go to File information > Lock. (Note that you will also be unable to make edits until you unlock the file.) Enable upload conversions to make .docx files into compatible Google filesAnother feature that saves a few clicks is auto-conversion of external files into Google formats. This is especially useful if you frequently receive documents from Microsoft users in .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx formats. Instead of manually converting each time, go to Settings > General, scroll down to Uploads, and toggle on Convert uploads to Google Docs editor format. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Editable Drive files allow you to easily highlight and leave comments on text, but you can do the same for other files while in preview mode, which is useful for providing feedback on visuals, layouts and design without downloading and opening in a separate program. Double-click to open any image or PDF preview and tap the Comment icon at the top. Select the area you want to leave feedback on and add your comment. Use advanced search operators to quickly find buried filesMy personal Drive is a bit of a mess, making it hard to find older files I've forgotten the names of without scrolling back through a very long list of unorganized items. Advanced search operators are part of the solution because they allow you to narrow down by file type, owner, and date. Enter terms like type:, owner:, and before: or after: into the search bar followed by your parameters. Drive's organizational structure is very basic—it'll show you suggested files and folders on your Home tab, but the My Drive tab is alphabetical by default with options for sorting by date modified. You can obviously create folders and move files around (including with the shortcuts hack described above), but it may also be useful to create a dynamic "hub" for quick access to files that are related, such as for a work project or a specific vacation. Paid Workspace users have a Priority tab, which collates to 25 files from anywhere in Drive without moving them from their original locations. Free users can star items or create a master Docs file and embed file tiles using the "@" menu. Use the Drive scanner to quickly digitize receipts and printed documents You don't actually need yet another app for document scanning: Google Drive has that feature built in, so both iPhone and Android users can quickly digitize printed material to Drive simply by using their device's camera. Open the Drive app and select the Scan icon or the (+), then hit Scan document. Google will make minor enhancements, then you can select the name and destination and hit Upload. From there, your scanned receipts, contracts, and other files are searchable just like anything else in your Drive.
